description: I’m a Software Engineering student at SMIU, Karachi, passionate about building innovative software products and solving real-world problems using technology. My interests include Python, Django REST Framework, FastAPI, AI/ML, and generative AI. I enjoy turning ideas into practical solutions and collaborating with people who are motivated to learn, build, and grow.
summary:
Crop-Watch AI is a simple, picture-based web app that helps farmers in Pakistan choose crop rotations that save water, protect soil and cope with a changing climate. A farmer opens it on a phone, and the app finds their farm and compares their current crops with alternative crop plans. It uses NASA Earth observations: POWER weather, GPM rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS green cover and land temperature, GRACE groundwater and SRTM elevation, plus SoilGrids soil data and FAO crop science.

Each plan gets a clear score with plain-word meters for water need, weather safety and soil health, weighted by the farmer’s own priorities. The app explains why each option was suggested, shows the evidence and the data gaps, and flags risks needing local review. It also checks this week’s crop risk, shows 20 years of past seasons and highlights when fields lie bare.

This matters because farmers face hotter seasons, scarce water and declining soil, yet must choose crops without seeing these risks. Crop-Watch AI turns complex satellite data into decisions any farmer can understand, supporting, not replacing, their judgement.
details:
What it does and how it works

Crop-Watch AI helps farmers compare crop rotations and choose the one that best fits their land, water and goals. A farmer opens the app on a phone and it finds the farm using the phone’s location, a district list or a tap on the map. It then:

  1. Shows the farm’s weather. The last 30 days, compared with the past year, using simple meters and a monthly rain and temperature chart.
  2. Compares crop plans. The farmer’s current rotation (e.g. wheat → rice) is set against alternatives such as wheat → mung bean → maize. For each crop, the backend splits the season into growth stages (FAO-56) and checks every day against that stage’s limits for heat, cold, drought, waterlogging and disease-friendly weather. It also calculates irrigation need with the FAO Penman-Monteith method, plus soil-health indicators (legumes, bare-soil days, SoilGrids soil data) and income.
  3. Scores each plan out of 100, using the farmer’s own priorities (soil, water, income, climate safety). Each plan also gets plain-word meters and an explanation: why it was suggested, its benefits, the evidence, the data gaps, and what to check locally.
    • A weekly “Is my crop safe?” check.
    • 20 years of past seasons showing how often each risk struck.
    • A field calendar showing bare periods.
    • What-if weather (hotter or drier).
    • Farmer limits, such as available water and crops they can’t sell.
    • An interactive NASA map with date slider and colour keys.
    • A printable report and a Learn page.

NASA data used

  • NASA POWER: daily weather, from 1981.
  • GPM IMERG: rainfall.
  • SMAP: soil moisture.
  • MODIS: green cover (NDVI) and land surface temperature.
  • GRACE/GRACE-FO: groundwater trend.
  • SRTM/NASADEM: elevation.
  • NASA GIBS: map imagery.
  • ECOSTRESS and HLS: downloaded for testing; field-level use is planned.
  • Other data: SoilGrids, FAO-56 and FAOSTAT.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers face rising heat, falling groundwater and tired soil, but they choose crops without seeing these risks. Crop-Watch AI makes those risks visible in simple pictures. In our Multan example, swapping rice for mung bean and maize needed about 41% less irrigation water and added a soil-building legume. We aim to help farmers save water, improve soil health and lower climate risk, and to give agricultural advisors a shared, evidence-based tool for conversations with farmers.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite, with Leaflet maps. It’s responsive for phones, with HTTPS for location access.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI. The scoring engine has 100+ automated tests (pytest).
  • Data access: the NASA POWER API, NASA Earthdata Cloud OPeNDAP, AppEEARS, GIBS map tiles, and GRACE mascon processing with NumPy.
  • Design: Microsoft Fluent Emoji 3D illustrations (MIT licence).
  • Development help: Claude (AI coding assistant).
  • Hardware: a standard laptop. The app runs on any smartphone with a browser.

What makes it creative

  • Pictures, not numbers. Satellite data becomes crop pictures, meters and plain words like “Your wheat is at risk this week”.
  • Honest by design. The app never invents values. Missing data is left out and the score is marked “partial”, and the app warns when two NASA rain sources disagree.
  • It looks back and ahead. It replays 20 years of real weather on the farmer’s own sowing dates, and offers what-if scenarios for a hotter, drier future.
  • It combines sources. It brings together many NASA missions with soil and crop science in one farmer-friendly comparison.

Factors we considered

  • Farmers with little technical experience: a simple layout, large images, phone use and future local languages.
  • Scientific honesty: limits come from FAO and published research. Unsupported thresholds are shown as gaps, not guesses.
  • Data limits: NASA data describes an area (about 10–50 km), not a single field, and is history, not a forecast. We say this clearly in the app.
  • Local context: Pakistani crops, sowing calendars, acres as the unit, and groundwater stress.
  • The farmer decides: the tool supports farmers and advisors; it doesn’t replace them.
